fichas.title: Auditorium seating, sightlines, and layout
fichas.summary: Auditorium seating gradients are derived from sightlines. The text discusses full sight super-elevation on every second row, seating arranged in arcs, side-aisle steps, proscenium proportions, audience perception, and acoustic distribution. Tiered theatres should provide a sufficiently deep view of the stage from the uppermost level.
uses: Arrange seating to provide sightlines to the stage
Set seating gradients and aisle steps
Support audience alignment and mutual perception

straight line

The elevation (gradient) of the seating in the auditorium is
derived from the sight lines. The sight line construction applies
for all places in the auditorium (stalls, but also tiers) --7 0. It can
be assumed that the spectators sit sensibly and so only every
second row requires full sight super-elevation (12 em). Specialised
mathematical literature addresses problems of view in the theatre,
including, for example, the distribution of people's heights.
Rows of spectators should be positioned in arcs, not only for
better alignment toward the stage, but also to achieve a better
perception of each other (security effect) --7 8. The stepped side
aisle must rise 10-19 em and the tread must not be less than
26 em. The floor between the seats must be on the same level as
the adjacent aisle at the side.

fichas.title: Flexible experimental theatre spaces
fichas.summary: Neutral or open theatre spaces allow different arrangements of spectators and stage areas. The page describes mobile stage platforms and audience stands on a fixed floor, or technically more elaborate movable floor podiums. It gives capacity guidance and an example area calculation for the simpler option.
